claim: Most studies of auditory segregation have used relatively simple signals, in contrast to the complex acoustic environments we encounter everyday.
source: In contrast to the complex acoustic environments we encounter everyday, most studies of auditory segregation have used relatively simple signals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study, drawing on established knowledge about the field.

claim: Human listeners are remarkably sensitive to the emergence of coherent patterns ('figures') from overlapping 'background' signals.
source: In a series of experiments, we demonstrate that human listeners are remarkably sensitive to the emergence of such figures and can tolerate a variety of spectral and temporal perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the series of experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Human listeners can tolerate a variety of spectral and temporal perturbations when detecting coherent patterns from background signals.
source: In a series of experiments, we demonstrate that human listeners are remarkably sensitive to the emergence of such figures and can tolerate a variety of spectral and temporal perturbations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from experiments 3-6 which tested various perturbations.

claim: The observed behavior is consistent with the existence of automatic auditory segregation mechanisms that are highly sensitive to correlations across frequency and time.
source: This robust behavior is consistent with the existence of automatic auditory segregation mechanisms that are highly sensitive to correlations across frequency and time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing robust performance across various conditions.

claim: The observed behavior cannot be explained purely on the basis of adaptation-based models used to explain the segregation of deterministic narrowband signals.
source: The observed behavior cannot be explained purely on the basis of adaptation-based models used to explain the segregation of deterministic narrowband signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and comparison with existing models.

claim: The present results are consistent with the predictions of a model of auditory perceptual organization based on temporal coherence.
source: We show that the present results are consistent with the predictions of a model of auditory perceptual organization based on temporal coherence.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Temporal coherence plays a role as an organizational principle underlying auditory segregation.
source: Our data thus support a role for temporal coherence as an organizational principle underlying auditory segregation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: The separation of mixtures of sounds into perceptually distinct sound sources is a highly complex task.
source: Although we do it effortlessly, the separation of such mixtures of sounds into perceptually distinct sound sources is a highly complex task.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of auditory perception.

claim: The neural bases of auditory object formation and segregation still remain to be fully explained.
source: In spite of being a topic of intense investigation for several decades, the neural bases of auditory object formation and segregation still remain to be fully explained (Cherry, 1953; McDermott, 2009; Griffiths et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature reviews.

claim: A sequence of two pure tones alternating in time can 'stream' or segregate into two sources under certain conditions.
source: The most commonly used signal for probing auditory perceptual organization is a sequence of two pure tones alternating in time that, under certain conditions, can 'stream' or segregate into two sources (van Noorden, 1975; Bregman, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: Fishman and colleagues observed spatially segregated responses to two tones in the auditory cortex of macaques for large frequency differences and fast presentation rates.
source: For large frequency differences and fast presentation rates, which promote two distinct perceptual streams, they observed spatially segregated responses to the two tones.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fishman et al.'s work.

claim: The pattern of segregated cortical activation has been proposed to underlie the streaming percept.
source: This pattern of segregated cortical activation, proposed to underlie the streaming percept, has since been widely replicated (e.g., Bee and Klump, 2004; 2005; Micheyl et al., 2007a; Bidet-Caulet and Bertrand, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to replication studies.

claim: Segregated cortical activation has been attributed to basic physiological principles of frequency selectivity, forward masking and neural adaptation.
source: This pattern of segregated cortical activation, proposed to underlie the streaming percept, has since been widely replicated (e.g., Bee and Klump, 2004; 2005; Micheyl et al., 2007a; Bidet-Caulet and Bertrand, 2009) and attributed to basic physiological principles of frequency selectivity, forward masking and neural adaptation (Fishman and Steinschneider, 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fishman and Steinschneider's work.

claim: These physiological properties contribute to stream segregation by promoting the activation of distinct neuronal populations in the primary auditory cortex (A1) that are well separated along the tonotopic axis.
source: These properties are considered to contribute to stream segregation by promoting the activation of distinct neuronal populations in the primary auditory cortex (A1) that are well separated along the tonotopic axis (McCabe and Denham, 1997; Carlyon, 2004; Micheyl et al., 2007a; Moore and Gockel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Human imaging studies support the correspondence between the streaming percept and the underlying neural activity in A1.
source: Human imaging studies that directly correlated the perceptual representation of streaming sequences with brain responses also support the correspondence between the streaming percept and the underlying neural activity in A1 (Gutschalk et al., 2005; Snyder et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2007; Cusack, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple imaging studies.

claim: Similar effects have been demonstrated in the auditory nerve, suggesting that processes contributing to segregation might occur earlier in the ascending auditory pathway.
source: However, similar effects have also been demonstrated in the auditory nerve, suggesting that processes contributing to segregation might occur earlier in the ascending auditory pathway rather than be mediated exclusively by the auditory cortex (Beauvois and Meddis, 1991; Pressnitzer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference from those studies.

claim: The streaming paradigm uses relatively simple, temporally regular narrowband signals which do not capture the rich spectrotemporal complexity of natural acoustic scenes.
source: A major drawback of the streaming paradigm is that it uses relatively simple, temporally regular narrowband signals which do not capture the rich spectrotemporal complexity of natural acoustic scenes.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Kidd and colleagues developed a spectrally rich signal referred to as the 'informational masking' (IM) stimulus.
source: Moving beyond streaming, Kidd and colleagues developed a spectrally rich signal referred to as the 'informational masking' (IM) stimulus (Kidd et al., 1994, 1995, 2011; Kidd and Mason, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kidd et al.'s work.

claim: Informational masking refers to a type of non-energetic or central masking that is associated with an increase in detection thresholds due to stimulus uncertainty and target-masker similarity.
source: IM refers to a type of non-energetic or central masking that is associated with an increase in detection thresholds due to stimulus uncertainty and target-masker similarity that is distinct from peripheral energetic masking (Pollack, 1975; Durlach et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Target detection in informational masking experiments is critically dependent on the width of the spectral protection region and the 'density' of the maskers.
source: Results demonstrate that target detection is critically dependent on the width of the spectral protection region, and the 'density' of the maskers (Micheyl et al., 2007b; Gutschalk et al., 2008; Elhilali et al., 2009b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Informational masking has been hypothesized to rely on the same adaptation-based mechanisms as proposed in the context of simple streaming signals.
source: Results demonstrate that target detection is critically dependent on the width of the spectral protection region, and the 'density' of the maskers (Micheyl et al., 2007b; Gutschalk et al., 2008; Elhilali et al., 2009b), and has been hypothesized to rely on the same adaptation-based mechanisms as proposed in the context of simple streaming signals (Micheyl et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Micheyl et al.'s work.

claim: Sounds we are required to segregate in everyday life are often broadband with multiple frequency components that are temporally correlated and overlap with other signals in the environment.
source: In contrast, the sounds we are required to segregate in everyday life are distinct from the narrowband targets used in streaming and IM paradigms; they are often broadband with multiple frequency components that are temporally correlated and overlap with other signals in the environment (McDermott and Simoncelli, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When two tones in a streaming signal are presented synchronously, listeners perceive the sequence as one stream irrespective of the frequency separation between the two tones.
source: Recently, Elhilali et al. (2009a) demonstrated that when the two tones in a streaming signal are presented synchronously, listeners perceive the sequence as one stream irrespective of the frequency separation between the two tones, a result that is inconsistent with predictions based on adaptation-based models.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elhilali et al.'s work.

claim: Temporal coherence between different elements in the scene is essential for segregation such that temporally incoherent patterns tend to result in a segregated percept while temporal coherence promotes integration.
source: Instead, the authors argued that in addition to separation in feature space, temporal coherence between different elements in the scene is essential for segregation such that temporally incoherent patterns tend to result in a segregated percept while temporal coherence promotes integration (Shamma et al., 2011; Fishman and Steinschneider, 2010b; Micheyl et al., 2013a,b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The SFG stimulus consists of coherent ('figure') and randomly varying ('background') components that overlap in spectrotemporal space and vary only in their statistics of fluctuation.
source: To investigate systematically the emergence of an auditory object from a random stochastic background, we developed a new stimulus (Stochastic figure-ground; SFG) consisting of coherent ('figure') and randomly varying ('background') components that overlap in spectrotemporal space and vary only in their statistics of fluctuation (Figure 1A; Teki et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the stimulus design used in the experiments, supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The components comprising the figure vary from trial to trial so that it can be extracted only by integrating across both frequency and time.
source: The components comprising the figure vary from trial to trial so that it can be extracted only by integrating across both frequency and time.
evidence: This describes a key design feature of the stimulus.

claim: In experiment 1, listeners showed a clear effect of increasing coherence and duration on figure detection performance.
source: The results (Figure 2A) show a clear effect of increasing coherence and duration.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Listeners achieved mean hit rates of 93 ± 2% for the most salient coherence/duration combination in experiment 1.
source: Hit rates (not shown) mirror d′ with listeners achieving mean hit rates of 93 ± 2% for the most salient coherence/duration combination.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 1.

claim: The patterns in experiment 1 were very brief (longest figure duration was 7 chords or 350 ms), yet very high levels of performance were observed.
source: It is notable that the patterns were very brief (longest figure duration was 7 chords or 350 ms), yet very high levels of performance were observed (and without extensive practice).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The high performance without extensive practice is consistent with the idea that this task taps low-level, finely tuned segregation mechanisms.
source: This is consistent with the idea that this task based on the SFG stimulus taps low-level, finely tuned segregation mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: A global power increase per se associated with the emergence of the figure can be discounted as a potential cue because 'figure-absent' and 'figure-present' signals were controlled for overall number of components.
source: Since 'figure-absent' and 'figure-present' signals were controlled for overall number of components (see 'Materials and methods'), a global power increase per se associated with the emergence of the figure, can be discounted as a potential cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: In experiment 2, for a figure duration of 4 chords (200 ms), listeners had difficulty with the discrimination task (d′ = 0.31 ± 0.18; not significantly different from 0: p=0.12, t = 1.72).
source: Results (Figure 2B) indicate that for the very short figure duration (4 chords, or 200 ms) listeners had difficulty with this discrimination task (d′ = 0.31 ± 0.18; not significantly different from 0: p=0.12, t = 1.72)
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: In experiment 2, performance increased significantly for a figure duration of 8 chords (400 ms; d′ = 1.75 ± 0.34).
source: Results (Figure 2B) indicate that for the very short figure duration (4 chords, or 200 ms) listeners had difficulty with this discrimination task (d′ = 0.31 ± 0.18; not significantly different from 0: p=0.12, t = 1.72), but that performance increased significantly for a figure duration of 8 chords (400 ms; d′ = 1.75 ± 0.34)
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, performance reached ceiling for a figure duration of 12 chords (600 ms; d′ = 2.93 ± 0.26).
source: Results (Figure 2B) indicate that for the very short figure duration (4 chords, or 200 ms) listeners had difficulty with this discrimination task (d′ = 0.31 ± 0.18; not significantly different from 0: p=0.12, t = 1.72), but that performance increased significantly for a figure duration of 8 chords (400 ms; d′ = 1.75 ± 0.34) and reached ceiling for a figure duration of 12 chords (600 ms; d′ = 2.93 ± 0.26).
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 2.

claim: The pattern of results in experiment 2 indicates that figure detection in these stimuli is associated with a segregation mechanism whereby coherent components are grouped together as a distinct perceptual object.
source: This pattern of results indicates that figure detection in these stimuli is associated with a segregation mechanism whereby coherent components are grouped together as a distinct perceptual object.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 2.

claim: It is difficult to account for listeners' performance in experiments 1 and 2 based on standard, adaptation-based models proposed in the context of the streaming paradigm.
source: It is difficult to account for listeners' performance in experiments 1 and 2 based on the standard, adaptation-based models proposed in the context of the streaming paradigm (Micheyl et al., 2007a; Fishman and Steinschneider, 2010a).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the data with existing models.

claim: The figure and background in the SFG stimuli overlap in frequency space, challenging segregation based on activation of spatially distinct neuronal populations in A1.
source: The figure and background in the SFG stimuli overlap in frequency space, thus challenging segregation based on activation of spatially distinct neuronal populations in A1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stimulus design and knowledge of neural mechanisms.

claim: Performance strongly depends on the number of simultaneously repeating frequency components, suggesting a mechanism that is able to integrate across widely spaced frequency channels.
source: Furthermore, the data clearly indicate that performance strongly depends on the number of simultaneously repeating frequency components, suggesting a mechanism that is able to integrate across widely spaced frequency channels, an element missing in previous models based on streaming.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The psychophysical data are consistent with a recently proposed model of auditory object formation based on analysis of temporal coherence.
source: Instead, the psychophysical data are consistent with a recently proposed model of auditory object formation based on analysis of temporal coherence (Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and citation to the temporal coherence model.

claim: The temporal coherence model is based on the idea that a perceptual 'stream' emerges when a group of (frequency) channels are coherently activated against the backdrop of other uncorrelated channels.
source: The temporal coherence model is based on the idea that a perceptual 'stream' emerges when a group of (frequency) channels are coherently activated against the backdrop of other uncorrelated channels (Shamma and Micheyl, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the model supported by citation.

claim: The temporal coherence model postulates that the figure becomes progressively more salient with more correlated tones in the different frequency channels.
source: The temporal coherence model postulates that the figure becomes progressively more salient with more correlated tones in the different frequency channels.
evidence: This is a description of the model's predictions.

claim: The model successfully accounted for the behavioral data in that an average cross-correlation based measure was able to systematically distinguish 'figure-present' from 'figure-absent' stimuli in a manner that mirrored the behavioral responses.
source: The model successfully accounted for the behavioral data in that, an average cross-correlation based measure was able to systematically distinguish 'figure-present' from 'figure-absent' (or background) stimuli in a manner that mirrored the behavioral responses.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The model's measure of temporal coherence showed a similar profile and increased with the coherence and the duration of the figure for the different experimental conditions.
source: The model's measure of temporal coherence showed a similar profile and increased with the coherence and the duration of the figure for the different experimental conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: This constitutes the first demonstration of the validity of the temporal coherence model for segregation in complex acoustic scenes.
source: This constitutes the first demonstration of the validity of the temporal coherence model for segregation in complex acoustic scenes.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the modeling results.

claim: In experiment 3, listeners achieved hit rates of 92 ± 3% for the highest coherence/duration combination used.
source: Behavioral results (Figure 4A) reveal good performance, as in experiment 1. Listeners achieved hit rates of 92 ± 3% for the highest coherence/duration combination used.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 3.

claim: In experiment 3, an ANOVA revealed no significant effect of condition (50 ms vs 25 ms chords) on performance (F1,15 = 2; p=0.174).
source: An ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (50 ms vs 25 ms chords) as a between-subject factor revealed no significant effect of condition (F1,15 = 2; p=0.174)
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data from experiment 3.

claim: Performance in experiment 3 largely depends on the number of repeating chords irrespective of the time scale.
source: An ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (50 ms vs 25 ms chords) as a between-subject factor revealed no significant effect of condition (F1,15 = 2; p=0.174), suggesting that performance largely depends on the number of repeating chords irrespective of the time scale.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis of experiment 3.

claim: In experiment 3, correlations across the spectrogram channels remained significant but occurred at higher rates than in experiment 1 (40 Hz vs 20 Hz).
source: Finally, as expected, model predictions were consistent with the experimental findings. Thus, correlations across the spectrogram channels remained significant, but now occurred at higher rates than in experiment 1 (40 Hz vs 20 Hz), reflecting the faster rate of tone presentations in the figure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is from the modeling results for experiment 3.

claim: In experiment 4, performance was robust with maximum hit-rates of 0.97 and 0.83 obtained for figures with coherence equal to 8 and duration equal to 7 for the two ramp levels of 2 and 5 respectively.
source: Performance in these experiments was robust (maximum hit-rates of 0.97 and 0.83 were obtained for figures with coherence equal to 8 and duration equal to 7 for the two ramp levels of 2 and 5 respectively)
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 4, an ANOVA revealed a significant effect of condition (repeating vs ramp size 2 vs ramp size 5): F2,25 = 19; p<0.001.
source: Performance in these experiments was robust (maximum hit-rates of 0.97 and 0.83 were obtained for figures with coherence equal to 8 and duration equal to 7 for the two ramp levels of 2 and 5 respectively) and a comparison with experiment 1 using an ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (repeating vs ramp size 2 vs ramp size 5) as a between-subject factor revealed a significant effect of condition: F2,25 = 19; p<0.001.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data from experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 4, performance was significantly worse for the ramp = 5 vs ramp = 2 condition (F1,18 = 21, p<0.001).
source: Performance was significantly worse for the ramp = 5 vs ramp = 2 condition (F1,18 = 21, p<0.001)
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data from experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 4, listeners exhibited above-chance performance even for the steeper slope (ramp = 5).
source: Performance was significantly worse for the ramp = 5 vs ramp = 2 condition (F1,18 = 21, p<0.001), but, remarkably, listeners exhibited above-chance performance even for the steeper slope.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data of experiment 4.

claim: The segregation mechanisms are more susceptible to spectral than temporal perturbations but can still integrate over dynamically changing, rather than fixed, figure components.
source: This suggests that the segregation mechanisms in question are more susceptible to spectral than temporal perturbations (as in experiments 3, and 6 below) but can still integrate over dynamically changing, rather than fixed, figure components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiments 3, 4, and 6.

claim: In experiment 4, the optimal rate at which the correlations occurred was slightly lower (at 10 Hz) than that of experiment 1 (20 Hz).
source: Finally, as with previous experiments, there were significant correlations among the channels predicting the saliency of the figure. However, the optimal rate at which the correlations occurred here was slightly lower (at 10 Hz; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) than that of experiment 1 (20 Hz), perhaps because two 50 ms chords are integrated as a single unit to define the ramp.
evidence: This is from the modeling results for experiment 4 with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: In experiment 5, results show a marked effect of coherence and duration, with performance improving with increasing salience of the figures.
source: Similar to previous experiments, the results (Figure 4C) show a marked effect of coherence and duration, and performance improved with increasing salience of the figures with listeners reaching hit rates of 89 ± 5% for the most salient condition.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 5, listeners reached hit rates of 89 ± 5% for the most salient condition.
source: Similar to previous experiments, the results (Figure 4C) show a marked effect of coherence and duration, and performance improved with increasing salience of the figures with listeners reaching hit rates of 89 ± 5% for the most salient condition.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 5, an ANOVA yielded no significant effect of condition (with background vs no background): F1,16 = 0.033; p=0.859.
source: To evaluate behavior with respect to experiment 1, an ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (with background vs no background) as a between-subject factor was used which yielded no significant effect of condition: F1,16 = 0.033; p=0.859
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data from experiment 5.

claim: The 'background-only' chords which preceded the figure did not affect performance in experiment 5.
source: To evaluate behavior with respect to experiment 1, an ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (with background vs no background) as a between-subject factor was used which yielded no significant effect of condition: F1,16 = 0.033; p=0.859, suggesting that the 'background-only' chords which preceded the figure did not affect performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis of experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 5, modeling replicated the results of experiment 1 in that the correlations increased with the coherence and duration of the figure and showed maximum response at 20 Hz.
source: Modeling for this experiment replicated the results of experiment 1 in that the correlations increased with the coherence and duration of the figure and showed maximum response at 20 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), corresponding to the rate of presentation of the chords comprising the figure.
evidence: This is from the modeling results for experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 6a, results show good behavioral performance with maximum hit rate of 0.93 obtained for the most salient condition.
source: The results (Figure 4D) show good behavioral performance (maximum hit rate of 0.93 was obtained for the most salient condition) which varied parametrically with the coherence and duration of the figure.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 6a.

claim: In experiment 6a, performance varied parametrically with the coherence and duration of the figure.
source: The results (Figure 4D) show good behavioral performance (maximum hit rate of 0.93 was obtained for the most salient condition) which varied parametrically with the coherence and duration of the figure.
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 6a.

claim: In experiment 6a, an ANOVA revealed no significant effect of condition (50 ms repeating chords vs 50 ms chords alternating with white noise): F1,17 = 0.004; p=0.953.
source: An ANOVA with coherence and duration as within-subject factors and experimental condition (50 ms repeating chords vs 50 ms chords alternating with white noise) as a between-subject factor revealed no significant effect of condition (F1,17 = 0.004; p=0.953).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data from experiment 6a.

claim: Interleaving noise bursts between successive chords does not affect performance in experiment 6a.
source: Interleaving the noise bursts between successive chords does not therefore affect performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis of experiment 6a.

claim: In experiment 6a, model predictions are broadly consistent with the findings in that detection became easier with more coherent tones and with longer figure intervals.
source: Model predictions in this experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F) are broadly consistent with the findings in that detection became easier with more coherent tones, and with longer figure intervals.
evidence: This is from the modeling results for experiment 6a.

claim: In experiment 6a, the noise weakens but does not eliminate the correlation among the tones, at least when computed at slower rates.
source: The reason is simply because the noise weakens but does not eliminate the correlation among the tones, at least when computed at slower rates.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the modeling results.

claim: In experiment 6b, results indicate robust performance for all durations of noise up to 300 ms.
source: Results (Figure 4E) indicate robust performance for all durations of noise up to 300 ms
evidence: This is experimental data from experiment 6b.

claim: In experiment 6b, listeners showed supra-threshold performance (d′ = 1.00 ± 0.30; significantly different from 0: p=0.01; t = 3.29) for a noise duration of 500 ms.
source: Results (Figure 4E) indicate robust performance for all durations of noise up to 300 ms and surprisingly, supra-threshold performance (d′ = 1.00 ± 0.30; significantly different from 0: p=0.01; t = 3.29) for a noise duration of 500 ms.
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis from experiment 6b.

claim: The remarkable ability of listeners to integrate coherent patterns over 3 s long (in the case of 500 ms noise bursts) suggests that the underlying higher-order mechanisms are very robust over such long time windows.
source: This remarkable ability of listeners to integrate coherent patterns over 3 s long (in the case of 500 ms noise bursts) suggests that the underlying higher-order mechanisms are very robust over such long time windows.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data of experiment 6b.

claim: Model predictions of experiment 6b findings are still possible if correlations are measured over longer windows (or slower rates—e.g., 3.33 Hz).
source: Model predictions of these findings are still possible if correlations are measured over longer windows (or slower rates—e.g., 3.33 Hz as in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is from the modeling results for experiment 6b.

claim: Temporal windows of integration as long as 500 ms have rarely been reported in the context of auditory object formation in complex scenes.
source: Temporal windows of integration, as long as 500 ms, have rarely been reported in the context of auditory object formation in complex scenes such as those examined here.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: The results suggest the existence of a central mechanism that is not affected by interfering broadband noise that integrates repeating pure tone components as belonging to a distinct object over multiple time scales.
source: The results suggest the existence of a central mechanism that is not affected by interfering broadband noise that integrates repeating pure tone components as belonging to a distinct object over multiple time scales.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of experiment 6b.

claim: The long temporal windows implicate cortical mechanisms at or beyond primary auditory cortex.
source: The long temporal windows here implicate cortical mechanisms at or beyond primary auditory cortex (see e.g., Overath et al., 2008 demonstrating a range of 'cortical windows' between 20 ms and 300 ms).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fast detection with minimal training of the SFG stimulus was demonstrated.
source: We demonstrate fast detection with minimal training of a novel figure-from-ground stimulus comprising an overlapping figure and ground segment where, like natural stimuli, the figure has multiple components that are temporally coherent: they start and stop together.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Such figures can be detected as objects that can be distinguished, consistent with a high-level mechanism for object detection as opposed to the simple detection of frequency or modulation cues.
source: We show that such figures can be detected as objects that can be distinguished, consistent with a high-level mechanism for object detection as opposed to the simple detection of frequency or modulation cues (experiment 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiment 2.

claim: The mechanism scales in time, in that detection depends on the number of components over time rather than their absolute duration.
source: The mechanism scales in time, in that detection depends on the number of components over time rather than their absolute duration (experiment 3)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiment 3.

claim: The mechanism can still operate if the object is defined by slowly changing frequency trajectories rather than a fixed set of frequencies.
source: The mechanism scales in time, in that detection depends on the number of components over time rather than their absolute duration (experiment 3) and can still operate if the object is defined by slowly changing frequency trajectories rather than a fixed set of frequencies (experiment 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiment 4.

claim: The mechanism is robust to interruption of the figure by interleaved noise.
source: It is robust to interruption of the figure by interleaved noise (experiment 5)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiment 5 (note: the text says experiment 5 but likely refers to experiment 6a based on the description).

claim: The mechanism can operate over a remarkably long timescale.
source: It is robust to interruption of the figure by interleaved noise (experiment 5) and can operate over a remarkably long timescale (experiment 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of experiment 6.

claim: Modeling based on temporal coherence demonstrated a similar profile to the behavioral results.
source: Modeling based on temporal coherence demonstrated a similar profile to the behavioral results and constitutes the first demonstration of the compatibility of the temporal coherence model with segregation in complex acoustic scenes.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The temporal coherence model proposes that segregation is determined not only based on separation in feature-space but rather by the temporal relationship between different elements in the scene.
source: The temporal coherence model proposes that segregation is determined not only based on separation in feature-space but rather by the temporal relationship between different elements in the scene, such that temporally coherent elements are grouped together, while temporally incoherent channels with independent fluctuation profiles are perceived as belonging to separate sources (Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the model supported by citation.

claim: The temporal coherence model incorporates two stages: a feature analysis stage and a temporal coherence analysis stage.
source: Specifically, the model incorporates two stages: firstly, a feature analysis stage that performs multidimensional feature analysis by distinct populations of neurons in the auditory cortex that are tuned to a range of temporal modulation rates and spectral resolution scales.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Elhilali et al. showed that a pair of synchronous repeating tones produces the same coherent pattern of modeled central activity as a single stream irrespective of the frequency separation between them.
source: Elhilali et al. carried out work implicating a critical role for temporal coherence in the assignment of common elements within a stream: they showed that a pair of synchronous repeating tones produces the same coherent pattern of modeled central activity as a single stream irrespective of the frequency separation between them, suggesting that temporal coherence is an important factor governing segregation (Elhilali et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elhilali et al.'s work.

claim: Direct neurophysiological recordings from ferret auditory cortex showed that synchronous and alternating cortical responses were equally segregated despite their perceptual differences.
source: This was substantiated by direct neurophysiological recordings from ferret auditory cortex which showed that synchronous and alternating cortical responses were equally segregated despite their perceptual differences, and hence that the temporal factors are more important in inducing the one and two streams percept (Shamma and Micheyl, 2010; Pressnitzer et al., 2011; Shamma et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Temporal factors are more important in inducing the one and two streams percept than spatial segregation.
source: This was substantiated by direct neurophysiological recordings from ferret auditory cortex which showed that synchronous and alternating cortical responses were equally segregated despite their perceptual differences, and hence that the temporal factors are more important in inducing the one and two streams percept (Shamma and Micheyl, 2010; Pressnitzer et al., 2011; Shamma et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the neurophysiological data supported by citations.

claim: The modeling results suggest that temporal coherence is modulated as a function of the coherence and the duration of the figure in a manner similar to the modulation of figure detection performance.
source: In the case of the more complex SFG stimuli, the modeling results suggest that temporal coherence is modulated as a function of the coherence and the duration of the figure in a manner similar to the modulation of figure detection performance.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The data suggest temporal coherence as a correlate of stimulus salience by which the brain picks out the most important sounds in busy auditory scenes.
source: The data suggest temporal coherence as a correlate of stimulus salience by which the brain picks out the most important sounds in busy auditory scenes: a process that may not be computed by dedicated structures but could be achieved by binding across distributed feature channels without significant changes in ensemble activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Similar accounts of binding in vision based on coherence of the temporal structure have been put forward previously.
source: Similar accounts of binding in vision based on coherence of the temporal structure have been put forward previously (e.g., Sporns et al., 1991; Alais et al., 1998; Blake and Lee, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to visual neuroscience literature.

claim: It is still not known how temporal coherence may be computed and which brain areas perform these computations.
source: It is still not known how temporal coherence may be computed and which brain areas perform these computations.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Temporal coherence may be implemented by neurons that show strong sensitivity to temporal coherence across distant frequency channels, or by neurons that act as multiplexers and are more selective to particular combinations of inputs.
source: Temporal coherence may be implemented by neurons that show strong sensitivity to temporal coherence across distant frequency channels, or by neurons that act as multiplexers and are more selective to particular combinations of inputs (Elhilali et al., 2009a; Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Elhilali et al. were unable to demonstrate cells sensitive to temporal coherence in the primary auditory cortex of passively listening ferrets but have preliminary evidence in behaving ferrets.
source: Elhilali et al. (2009a) sought such cells in the primary auditory cortex of the ferret but were unable to demonstrate any in passively listening animals but have preliminary evidence in behaving ferrets (Shamma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elhilali et al.'s work.

claim: Previous brain imaging studies have identified activity in A1 that was correlated with the streaming percept.
source: Although previous brain imaging studies have identified activity in A1 that was correlated with the streaming percept (e.g., Gutschalk et al., 2005; Snyder et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: No evidence of modulation of BOLD signal in A1 as a function of figure emergence was found in a passive listening paradigm using the SFG stimulus.
source: Although previous brain imaging studies have identified activity in A1 that was correlated with the streaming percept (e.g., Gutschalk et al., 2005; Snyder et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2007), we found no evidence of modulation of BOLD signal in A1 as a function of figure emergence in a passive listening paradigm (Teki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Activity in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) was found to be strongly modulated by the salience of the figure, similar to the modulation of temporal coherence.
source: However, we found activity in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) to be strongly modulated by the salience of the figure, similar to the modulation of temporal coherence observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The IPS activation likely reflects bottom-up stimulus-driven processing of figures.
source: The IPS activation likely reflect bottom-up stimulus-driven processing of figures and is consistent with accumulating literature which suggests that areas outside the conventional auditory system, such as the parietal cortex may have a role in auditory segregation (Cusack, 2005; Dykstra et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to literature.

claim: Areas outside the conventional auditory system, such as the parietal cortex, may have a role in auditory segregation.
source: The IPS activation likely reflect bottom-up stimulus-driven processing of figures and is consistent with accumulating literature which suggests that areas outside the conventional auditory system, such as the parietal cortex may have a role in auditory segregation (Cusack, 2005; Dykstra et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: Attention influences segregation.
source: Although not relevant to the passive fMRI experiment (Teki et al., 2011), attention also influences segregation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The parietal cortex is in an ideal position to integrate both bottom-up auditory input and top-down attentional input from the prefrontal cortex.
source: In this regard, the parietal cortex is in an ideal position to integrate both bottom-up auditory input as it receives auditory input from the temporoparietal cortex (Pandya and Kuypers, 1969; Divac et al., 1977; Hyvärinen, 1982; Cohen, 2009) as well as top-down attentional input from the prefrontal cortex (Andersen et al., 1985; Barbas and Mesulam, 1981; Petrides and Pandya, 1984; Stanton et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: IPS is associated with both bottom-up and top-down attention and is a key structure implicated in saliency map models of visual search.
source: IPS is associated with both bottom-up and top-down attention and is a key structure implicated in saliency map models of visual search (Koch and Ullman, 1985; Itti and Koch, 2001; Walther and Koch, 2007) where low-level feature maps may combine with top-down cognitive biases to represent a global saliency map (Gottlieb et al., 1998; Geng and Mangun, 2009; Bisley and Goldberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to visual neuroscience literature.

claim: IPS has been implicated in mediating object representations, binding of sensory features within and across different modalities, as well as attentional selection.
source: IPS (and its monkey homologue) has been implicated in mediating object representations, binding of sensory features within and across different modalities, as well as attentional selection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IPS function.

claim: IPS may represent a neural correlate of the figure percept where the representation will depend on the salience of auditory figures.
source: We hypothesize that IPS may represent a neural correlate of the figure percept where the representation will depend on the salience of auditory figures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The perceptual representation in IPS depends on the computation of temporal coherence across multiple frequencies that are initially represented in the auditory cortex.
source: In our model, this perceptual representation depends on the computation of temporal coherence across multiple frequencies that are initially represented in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the model and imaging results.

claim: The SFG stimulus consists of a sequence of random chords, each 50 ms in duration with 0 ms inter-chord-interval, presented for a total duration of 2000 ms (40 consecutive chords).
source: Figure 1 presents examples of the SFG stimulus which consists of a sequence of random chords, each 50 ms in duration with 0 ms inter-chord-interval, presented for a total duration of 2000 ms (40 consecutive chords).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: Each chord in the SFG stimulus contains a random number (average: 10 and varying between 5 and 15) of pure tone components.
source: Each chord contains a random number (average: 10 and varying between 5 and 15) of pure tone components.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: The spectral components in the SFG stimulus are randomly selected from a set of 129 frequencies equally spaced on a logarithmic scale between 179 Hz and 7246 Hz.
source: The spectral components are randomly selected from a set of 129 frequencies equally spaced on a logarithmic scale between 179 Hz and 7246 Hz such that the separation between successive components is 1/24th of an octave.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: The onset and offset of each chord in the SFG stimulus are shaped by a 10 ms raised-cosine ramp.
source: The onset and offset of each chord are shaped by a 10 ms raised-cosine ramp.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: In half of the SFG stimuli, a random number of tones are repeated across a certain number of consecutive chords which results in the percept of a 'figure' that readily pops out of the random tonal background.
source: In half of these stimuli, a random number of tones are repeated across a certain number of consecutive chords (e.g., in Figure 1, four components marked by arrows are repeated across 6 chords) which results in the percept of a 'figure' that readily pops out of the random tonal background.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design and the perceptual effect.

claim: To eliminate correlation between the number of figure and background components, the figure was realized by first generating the random background and then adding additional, repeating components to the relevant chords.
source: To eliminate correlation between the number of figure and background components, the figure was realized by first generating the random background and then adding additional, repeating components to the relevant chords.
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation procedure to control for confounds.

claim: In 50% of the SFG stimuli (those containing no figure), additional tonal components were added over a variable number (2–7) of consecutive chords at the same time as when a figure would have appeared, but these components changed from chord to chord and did not form a coherent figure.
source: To avoid the problem that the interval containing the figure might, on average, also contain more frequency components, and to prevent listeners from relying on this feature in performing the figure detection task, the remaining 50% of the stimuli (those containing no figure) also included additional tonal components, which were added over a variable number (2–7) of consecutive chords at the same time as when a figure would have appeared. But these additional components changed from chord to chord and did not form a coherent figure.
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation procedure to control for confounds.

claim: The onset of the figure in the SFG stimulus was jittered between 15 and 20 chords (750–1000 ms) post stimulus onset.
source: The onset of the figure was jittered between 15 and 20 chords (750–1000 ms) post stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: All participants tested in this set of experiments reported normal hearing and had no history of audiological or neurological disorders.
source: All participants tested in this set of experiments reported normal hearing and had no history of audiological or neurological disorders.
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria.

source: Experimental procedures were approved by the research ethics committee of University College London (Project ID number: 1490/002), and written informed consent was obtained from each participant.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from each participant.
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the research ethics committee of University College London (Project ID number: 1490/002), and written informed consent was obtained from each participant.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures for the study.

claim: The temporal coherence model consists of two distinct stages: a first stage that simulates spectral analysis at the cochlea and temporal integration at the auditory cortex, and a second stage that incorporates coherence analysis.
source: The temporal coherence model consists of two distinct stages. The first stage takes the spectrogram of the stimulus as its input and simulates spectral analysis performed at the level of the cochlea and temporal integration at the level of the auditory cortex (Chi et al., 2005; Elhilali and Shamma, 2008; Elhilali et al., 2009a; Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the model structure supported by citations.

claim: Temporal integration in the model is achieved through a bank of bandpass filters that are tuned to different physiologically plausible parameters that capture the rich variety of spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) found in A1.
source: This temporal integration is achieved through a bank of bandpass filters that are tuned to different physiologically plausible parameters that capture the rich variety of spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) found in A1.
evidence: This describes the model implementation.

claim: The model uses a range of physiologically valid temporal modulation rates (from slow to fast: 2–32 Hz) and spectral resolution scales (narrow to broad: 0.125 to 8 cycles per octave).
source: This is realized by using a range of physiologically valid temporal modulation rates (from slow to fast: 2–32 Hz) and spectral resolution scales (narrow to broad: 0.125 to 8 cycles per octave).
evidence: This describes the model parameters.

claim: The coherence analysis stage of the model computes a 'windowed' correlation between each pair of channels by taking the product of the filter outputs corresponding to the different channels.
source: The next level of the model incorporates a 'coherence analysis' stage which computes a 'windowed' correlation between each pair of channels by taking the product of the filter outputs corresponding to the different channels.
evidence: This describes the model computation.

claim: A dynamic coherence matrix which consists of the cross-correlation values as a function of time is obtained from the model.
source: A dynamic coherence matrix which consists of the cross-correlation values as a function of time is thus obtained.
evidence: This describes the model output.

claim: The off-diagonal elements of the coherence matrix indicate the presence of coherence across different channels, that is, positively correlated activity.
source: The off-diagonal elements of the matrix indicate the presence of coherence across different channels, that is, positively correlated activity and offer insight into the perceptual representation of the stimulus.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the model output.
